speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Yet, international political turmoil, terrorism, threats and social division worldwide are pulling nations apart.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: To win popular votes, we see politicians in other countries playing up a variety of issues from religion to racism and trade protectionism.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This gives rise to riot, hate crimes and, even long after the political race is over, it leaves behind deep divisions among its people.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Apart from social differences, mistrust towards immigrants and fear of terrorism continue to plague and divide the likes of the US, Germany, France and so on.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The troubles of other multicultural countries, some closer to our nation, must serve as a stark reminder to Singaporeans that we must not take peace and harmony for granted.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our leaders who led the racial harmony movement were far-sighted.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Beyond tolerance, they urged us to understand and respect one another's background as well as religion.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I remember during the 1993 Malaysian Cup, the Singapore National Football Team played against Kedah and we won 2-0.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Singaporeans gathered by the busloads in Kuala Lumpur to support our national team.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many were shouting their hearts out at home in front of their television (TVs).

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The entire nation rejoiced in one voice, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We had a similar reaction last year when Joseph Schooling won the first Olympic Gold Medal for Singapore.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The entire nation was frozen and holding our breath during those 50.39 seconds.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Again, the nation celebrated the success, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Apart from sports that can bring Singaporeans together, there are many others.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: In March 2015, we all came together to mourn the passing of our beloved founding Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Although we are one of the youngest nations on earth, we have demonstrated and risen to the occasion to overcome our race, language and religion divides and come together as one people, one nation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The proliferation of Internet culture has blurred the lines between truth and lies.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is very convenient now to spread falsehood, with the purpose of inciting chaos and hatred.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Frequent exposure to inappropriate ideology, along with the climate of dissatisfaction, can lead to the breakdown of our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):   Madam, over the past few years, increasingly more support is being provided to workers from the professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs) group through various programmes and assistance schemes like training in reskilling, job matching and others.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think few countries in the world provide such assistance.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, it is understood that although there is help specifically targeted at PMETs, many may still experience uncertainty and doubt about their future within this challenging economic situation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so for those who lost their jobs or are employed in sectors or jobs that are impacted by the economy or have a bleak future.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I note that, for the Malay/Muslim community, many efforts have been done to help PMETs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, the Council on Education for Muslim Children (MENDAKI), together with several Malay/Muslim bodies, made efforts help this group.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister share what are the efforts and types of assistance that can be extended to this group?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Last November, this Chamber debated the Constitution of the Republic of Singapore (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One of the issues that received attention and was hotly debated was the recommendation to hold a Presidential Election reserved for a minority race.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Constitutional Commission made this recommendation because they felt the need to address the issue of perception that a minority race cannot assume the highest office in the land, that is, the office of President.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This Chamber and Singaporeans were divided into two groups: those who supported it and those who did not support it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Those who agreed with the recommendation for a Presidential Election reserved for minorities argued that it is necessary to do so in order to signify and represent Singapore's multiracial constitution.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For those who opposed, the argument is that its implementation will weaken the principle of meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I am also of the view that the decision to hold a reserved Presidential Election as an effort to address the issue of negative perceptions, shows that "where there is a will, there is a way." I have said many times before in this Chamber that among the aspirations or concerns of the Malay/Muslim community in Singapore is the sense or perception of discrimination that there are no equal and fair opportunities.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Minister Yaacob spoke about and acknowledges this concern.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: During a dialogue session organised by the Feedback Unit's Reaching Everyone for Active Citizenry @ Home (REACH), the Minister said in English that "The Malay community is concerned not just about the President, but also Malay Permanent Secretary, Malay General... because we want to see representation across the entire Singaporean life".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As I said before, Madam, "where there's a will, there's a way." I sincerely hope that the Government can do something to address the concerns of the community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   In order to be adaptable and future-ready, lifelong learning is a must for every individual.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This will allow us to easily transit to a new industry or improve what we are already doing.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: (In Malay):   SkillsFuture is more than just about providing SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Our hope is that the concept and objectives of SkillsFuture, including increasing awareness and fully taking advantage of this scheme, are understood by all Singaporeans, including Malay/Muslims.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: All levels of society should make use of this scheme, from housewives to students, workers and also entrepreneurs.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: However, in order for SkillsFuture to be truly beneficial for them, it will require an understanding and knowledge on the best way to use it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: A more focused help and guidance may be required by the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: For instance, students may need to know which roadmaps are relevant and which career paths will emerge.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Some may not have the confidence and need guidance.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad
text: Can the Minister provide the latest update on this effort?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   The Syariah Court is one of the major institutions for the Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This institution has overseen divorce matters since 1958 and, over the years, we have observed and continue to expect innovations and improvements in terms of its administration and management of duties in Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Last year, I asked about the review on the Court's processes and the application of technology, where possible.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Apart from improvements to the Court's processes and systems, it is also important to ensure there is an adequate and trained workforce in order to address future challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These include the community's demand for speedier processes, legal issues that are increasingly complex, and a more holistic service for families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What plans are being made to strengthen the capabilities of the Court's workforce, particularly in ensuring a continuous pipeline of talent who are suitable for service in the Syariah Court?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Last year, the Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs highlighted that the Syariah Court was improving its Court processes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe there is a need to continue to review the processes and incorporate the use of technology, where appropriate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Could the Minister share on any further plans currently being implemented or planned for the Syariah Court?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Also, it is important to develop the manpower and the capabilities of the officers serving in the Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Is there a viable talent pipeline in place such that there will always be capable people ready to serve in the Court?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   The Malay/Muslim community has excelled and achieved a lot of success in many fields.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: However, there are still some who are trapped in a vicious cycle.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: At the constituency level, a lot has been done to help this group, in terms of financial assistance, jobs, groceries, learning and many more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: At the national level, other channels of assistance are also being arranged.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: One other group comprises families that came about from divorces and reconstituted families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Apart from the assistance schemes mentioned earlier, there are other dynamics and family challenges within this group that need to be addressed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For this particular group, their problems sometimes get passed down from one generation to the next.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How can we help them escape the situation and break the cycle?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: What is the best way to engage them so that they can change their views and outlook that are negative and not progressive in nature, for the sake of their future?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   Our Malay/Muslim community has become increasingly more diverse and varied as our larger Singapore society becomes more globalised and complex.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other than matters related to faith, beliefs and practices, our Malay/Muslim community also needs to be prepared and to receive sufficient guidance in addressing global issues, such as xenophobia, racial and religious discrimination, threats of terrorism and misguided beliefs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are increasingly seeing more xenophobic and discriminatory acts and speeches taking place in the developed world, such as in the US, France, the Netherlands and Australia, against Muslims and people of colour and minority faiths, which have caused much concern.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our Malay/Muslim community in Singapore needs to be ready when faced with such situations fueled by hate so that we are able to counter them with intelligence, conviction, love and patience.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, there are numerous opportunities globally for us to learn new skills, develop our entrepreneurial spirit and get employment opportunities.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our mainstream school students are being prepared to be globally-ready and future-ready.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our full-time madrasah students would also need to expand their skillsets and knowledge base, beyond just being trained to be asatizahs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Can the Minister share how the Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) can help our asatizahs to be better equipped to address such global issues and also help our madrasah students to be globally-ready and future-ready?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Many Singaporeans I have met are supportive of this initiative.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister update the House on the progress of the scheme's implementation?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   Madam, there are three areas that I would like to bring to the Minister's attention regarding the support being provided to madrasah students.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, many Malay/Muslim residents lamented that they were unable to do so due to the quota.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Does MUIS have plans to request for an increase in this quota to meet the community's demand?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, could the Minister also share whether the performance of madrasah students in the national examinations have shown improvement over the last five years?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: (In Malay):   Last year, the Minister announced plans for Madrasah Al-Arabiah to have a new home in Toa Payoh.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: This is good news as the existing building is old and a makeover is long overdue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: However, what is important to me is the madrasah's environment and not merely its physical aspect.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: These days, mainstream schools that are part of the national education system are equipped with facilities and technology to keep up with the times and provide the children with the necessary exposure to the relevant technology.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Furthermore, how can the students and the school interact with and contribute to the heartland community around the area?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: (In Malay):   The Administration of Muslim Law Act (AMLA) is an Act that, among other things, makes provisions for the administration of MUIS, the Registry of Muslim Marriages (ROMM) and the Syariah Court.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is an important piece of legislation that sets the basis for matters relating to the administration of the Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Given that some time has passed since then, may I ask if there are plans to review and update this Act so that it adapts to present circumstances?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In particular, are there any plans to amend the provisions within AMLA and the Muslim Marriage and Divorce Rules (MMDR) that decide on matters relating to the processes of the Syariah Court?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: (In English): AMLA makes provision for three key institutions in the Malay/Muslim community, namely, MUIS, the Registry of Muslim Marriages and the Syariah Court, amongst other things.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Given that some time has passed since the last amendment, could the Minister-in-charge of Muslim Affairs update us on whether there are plans to amend AMLA?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In particular, are there any plans to review AMLA and MMDR to see if the provisions match the existing circumstances of the community as well as the current practice of the Syariah Court?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I believe that efforts can be put in place to further enhance the Syariah Court's delivery of services through a review of the Act and the Rules.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Issues, such as jurisdiction, the hukum process, the talak declaration process, may be some of the areas that the Court may wish to review.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It is useful to look at the existing procedures and forms and amend AMLA and MMDR accordingly to make the process more expedient to better serve the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, the number of private tuition centres that have sprung up in the CCs raise several questions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, are these private tuition centres offered subsidised rent for operating within the premises of the CCs and, if so, what is the basis for the subsidy?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If the private tuition centres are paying competitive market rent, then the question is: is it right for CCs to monetise the common space for private ends?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the communal activities that are being displaced by the tuition centres?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The more fundamental question is whether this contradicts the Government's education policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two years ago, then-Minister for Education Heng Swee Keat said, "Singapore needs to make the transformation from a 'scarcity mentality' that focuses on a single pathway to success to an 'abundance mentality' with multiple pathways".

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He was responding to concerns raised by Members of this House regarding Singapore's pervasive tuition culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: CCs should not be reinforcing this tuition culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The past year has seen a culmination of trends of many years in the making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Communities in many countries have become more fragmented, while social support systems are straining in the face of growing challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: However, I am confident we can find a way to remain resilient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Our community has worked hard in partnership with the Government and we have come far.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In a uniquely Singaporean way, we have embraced diversity and forged strong bonds with people of other races and religions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We can never be certain of the future, but we can be stronger if we look out for one another.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We can be confident of success if, together, we build a more resilient and confident community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: First, our community institutions will enhance efforts to develop a future-ready and resilient workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Second, we will strengthen and safeguard our families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Third, we will nurture a strong socio-religious sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To ride the transformation in our economy, we must work together to expand the opportunities for our community to be upskilled and ready for the jobs of the future.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Yayasan MENDAKI currently provides assistance to low-wage workers and their families through its subsidiary, MENDAKI SENSE.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: However, as Mr Zaqy Mohamad highlighted, we should also support the lower-middle income PMETs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This committee will focus on helping this group retrain and rebound from potential employment setbacks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: One area for improvement is the community's take-up of national skills-upgrading initiatives, such as SkillsFuture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: More can be done to explain and link them to SkillsFuture and other national schemes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We will push hard to encourage more to try and, for those who do, we want to support them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: One individual who worked hard and benefited from skills-upgrading is 34-year-old Dzahri Bin Dzulkifli.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Dzahri was an information technology (IT) Technician for six years before he took on an enhanced, multifaceted role as an information and communications technology (ICT) analyst and trainer.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To add value to his new role, Dzahri attended MENDAKI SENSE's International Computer Driving Licence (ICDL) course in 2016.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: He has completed six modules ranging from Basic to Advanced programmes, putting in hard work outside of work.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Dzahri is now into his fifth year in this role and continues to find meaning in what he does.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Dzahri's example shows that while training may not be easy and may not pay off immediately, it pays off with perseverance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To help workers like Dzahri, MENDAKI SENSE will step up its efforts, in partnership with Workforce SG and SkillsFuture SG, to provide good employment opportunities that resonate well with the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: But at the same time, more must be done to make continual learning and training a social norm or a natural impulse of our community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: So, as Mr Saktiandi Supaat has asked, how can we help grow this culture of lifelong learning?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This year marks MENDAKI's 35th anniversary (M35), which it will be celebrating through a series of initiatives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This is a pilot programme to promote e-learning among students in the MENDAKI Tuition Scheme (MTS) and to engage them beyond the usual three-hour weekly MTS sessions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Second, MENDAKI is producing the Keluarga Bestari book, a collaboration between MENDAKI and Singapore Press Holdings which features the success stories of Malay/Muslim families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We hope that these stories of ordinary and everyday heroes will inspire the rest of our community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Further, the sale of these books will contribute to the Educational Trust Fund, which supports the education of children from nursery up to the Institute of Technical Education (ITE).

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Third, MENDAKI will organise an Education Symposium to discuss the important positive role that parents must play in their children's development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: MENDAKI will be inviting 500 key stakeholders and national partners to discuss issues and research on early childhood education at the symposium.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I have outlined some of MENDAKI's plans to promote learning at an early age, but more work will also be done downstream.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamad asked for an update on MENDAKI's Future Ready Unit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Launched last year, the unit has conducted several engagement sessions to promote SkillsFuture, particularly among students and parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These efforts have reached out to over 1,000 students and young adults to better understand and support their aspirations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Moving forward, MENDAKI will run more of such programmes to forge a future-oriented mindset among our young.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It will also introduce a new Future First programme for Malay/Muslim students in the Higher National ITE Certificate (NITEC) courses this year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There are families facing socio-economic challenges and we must do all that we can to help them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef asked how Government agencies and community organisations have been coordinating efforts to better support the low-income and stepfamilies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: One way we do this is to nurture strong and stable families and ensure that the services we provide meet the needs of these families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Vista Sakinah will continue its good work for remarrying couples and stepfamilies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: One initiative involves tapping on our asatizahs, or religious teachers, who have relevant skills and good outreach.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We want to encourage our asatizahs to broaden how they can serve the social needs of our community, and remarriages and stepfamilies are one group which requires support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: One example is Ustaz Muhammad Hafiizh Rapiee, who has been conducting support sessions for stepfamilies since 2014.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To help Ustaz Hafiizh, Vista Sakinah familiarises him with the families' situations so that he can provide complementary religious guidance.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ustaz Hafiizh is currently one of 11 asatizahs engaged by Vista Sakinah.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Another example of the benefits of working together was MSF's collaboration with MUIS and MENDAKI in organising the 5th Engaging Hearts and Minds Seminar.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Held last October, and themed "Seeding Resilience for Our Children", the seminar shared trends and insights on contemporary child-raising from the sociological, religious and practice perspectives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Such sharing is important so that educators, social workers and asatizahs are able to better understand the families' needs and tailor their interventions accordingly.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked for an update on the Syariah Court's (SYC's) plans to improve its capabilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Over the next two to three years, SYC will be enhancing its case management system and processes to provide users with a more client-centric experience, with a focus on improving online services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: With these systemic improvements, SYC will better serve their clients.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It must, therefore, be staffed by capable people and open to a diversity of talents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The secondment is part of a broader collaboration between MUIS and SYC to ensure that there is a robust talent pipeline to lead our Muslim statutory institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: SYC will continue to tap on their services even after their retirement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This brings me to my third key thrust − growing a strong socio-religious sector.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The Singapore Muslim community draws strength and guidance from our asatizahs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In turn, our asatizahs have the responsibility to provide the community with sound religious guidance that is appropriate for our Singapore context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This is especially so amidst an increasingly diverse and vibrant socio-religious landscape, a point that Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar has also noted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: A key example of this is our Fatwa Committee, which has the responsibility of guiding Muslims on contemporary socio-religious issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Chaired by our Mufti, the committee comprises experienced local asatizahs who issue fatwas, or religious opinions, to help Singaporean Muslims understand and balance their religious and civic identities and obligations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In deliberating on a wide range of issues, the committee has also tapped on experts from diverse disciplines.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Our fatwas have endeavoured to help Singaporean Muslims stay true to the teachings of Islam while living out their lives in modern, secular and multicultural Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: At the inaugural Fatwa Conference on 11 February this year, our Mufti, Dr Mohamed Fatris Bakaram, said that "Finding answers to new questions is not as straightforward as conveniently saying, 'Let's go back to the Quran and Sunnah'…A responsible fatwa authority is one that provides guidance to real challenges faced by the community." He also cautioned against feeling contented with "the voluminous compilations of positive law produced by classical scholars however excellent these intellectual treasures might have been".

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I agree with the Mufti wholeheartedly and understand that the Fatwa Committee may, at times, depart from the positions of religious bodies elsewhere in the Muslim world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I hope that Singaporeans will appreciate the Committee's efforts in providing religious guidance that is contextually appropriate for the diversity in our Muslim community and in our multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: With this in mind, MUIS is developing a Fatwa Rulings Compilation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The first of five volumes was launched at the recent Fatwa Conference and is an important contribution to scholarship and as a source of public education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: MUIS also hopes that Singapore's experience at making progressive fatwas can contribute to the advancement of global Islamic jurisprudence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar asked how MUIS can help better equip our asatizahs to meet the needs of the community, while Dr Muhammad Faishal Ibrahim asked for an update on the mandatory ARS.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Registered asatizahs are assessed to have the minimum requirements to provide religious instruction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This system provides the community with greater assurance that those who offer religious guidance have the baseline qualifications and training.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It is not just about the asatizahs' paper qualifications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Their religious guidance must also be compatible with our cherished values and way of life in modern, multicultural Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Many of our asatizahs are graduates of the six full-time madrasahs offering primary, secondary and pre-university education to more than 3,500 madrasah students.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Madrasahs play an important role in developing future generations of asatizahs with strong grounding in both the religious and secular subjects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To Mr Zainal Sapari's question, the existing madrasah quota of 400 students per cohort has been able to produce the asatizahs needed to meet our community's needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: MUIS monitors these numbers and also looks at the competencies required.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To ensure that our asatizahs meet these competencies, it is imperative that we continuously focus on raising the quality of madrasah education and inspiring our students to do their best.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In the last few years, our madrasah students have improved their performance in the national examinations.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: More students are also qualifying for the Express stream.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These trends bode well for the future of our asatizah fraternity and Muslim institutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Teachers will also benefit from additional training funds and incentives that scale with their qualifications.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I would also like to share that MUIS will match the Government's assistance in the form of new student awards and teacher training grants for religious subjects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This partnership between the Government and the community will encourage our madrasah students and teachers to continue to improve themselves and be the best that they can be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As part of its wider support for the madrasah sector, MUIS is also developing a new Madrasah Al-Arabiah campus in Toa Payoh.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: MUIS has set aside $10 million for the new campus, with Madrasah Al-Arabiah engaging the community to co-fund the remainder.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: MUIS will consult the school's community on the campus design in the third quarter of 2017.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In response to Mr Amrin Amin's question, I would like to update that MBMF collections within the first six months of the revision have been healthy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The support for the changes to MBMF is an affirmation of the affluence of our community and of our spirit of self-help.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Through MBMF, we come together to build our mosques, strengthen our religious education and uplift Muslim families.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The rate revision last year will also help ensure that there are sufficient funds to pay for current and future mosque developments.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Mr Amrin Amin had asked for an update on the construction of the Yusof Ishak Mosque in Woodlands.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Funded by MBMF, the Yusof Ishak Mosque is the 26th mosque to be built under MUIS' Mosque Building Programme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: With a unique architectural design and a capacity to accommodate 4,500 congregants, the Yusof Ishak Mosque will be an institution that we can all be proud of.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Beyond building new mosques, various other upgrading works have also been carried out, such as the Sallim Mattar Mosque, Al-Falah Mosque, Al-Khair Mosque, Al-Muttaqin Mosque and a temporary prayer facility at Al-Istighfar Mosque.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Lastly, Madam, Ms Rahayu Mahzam asked for an update on plans to amend AMLA.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Our agencies have been working closely together to finetune this key legislation for our community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Allow me now to continue my speech in Malay.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: (In Malay):   Madam Chairman, in view of the uncertain global climate, the Malay/Muslim community has no option but to be prepared to continue adapting ourselves so that we can progress together with the other communities in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I believe that we are able to do it because we are in a good position as a result of our close partnership with the Government for over 50 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We are now more confident to face challenges.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I have mapped out three strategies to further strengthen our collective endeavours.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Thirdly, our socio-religious life will be enriched further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: With the expected slowdown in the country's economic growth, there is a need to upgrade the skills of Malay/Muslim workers at all levels.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Efforts to increase the community's awareness and encourage them to take advantage of national skills upgrading schemes like SkillsFuture, must be intensified.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Community organisations will work with the Government to ensure that Malay/Muslim workers can obtain better job opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Low-wage workers will continue to receive assistance from MENDAKI SENSE.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: However, we are also aware of the challenges faced by the lower-middle income group comprising PMETs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Among other things, they will receive help in retraining and making preparations in case they are retrenched.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In preparing for a more challenging future, we need to acquire and embrace the spirit of lifelong learning.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Therefore, Yayasan MENDAKI will focus on efforts to inculcate lifelong learning, in addition to empowering the community through education.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: On the occasion of MENDAKI's 35th anniversary, several initiatives will be introduced to achieve this objective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These include the launch of Digital Learning@MTS to encourage online learning for students from MTS; publishing a book titled "Secrets of Successful Families" that showcases success stories of Malay/Muslim families; and an Education Symposium to discuss the important role of parents in their children's development.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Hence, Malay/Muslim community organisations will continue to complement national programmes to strengthen the family institution.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: SYC, as an important institution that administers Muslim family law, will ensure that family interests will be a key priority.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The case management systems and processes at SYC will be enhanced to make it more user-friendly, especially by improving online services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: SYC also received two new Presidents last year, Ustaz Muhammad Fazalee Jaafar and Ustazah Raihanah Halid.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This collaboration between MUIS and SYC is part of the efforts to ensure a continuous flow of talent in order to strengthen the administration of Islamic institutions in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Last February, MUIS organised the inaugural Fatwa Conference to share how the institution of fatwa or Islamic legal rulings has guided our community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Since 1968, the Fatwa Committee has issued fatwa that touch on various aspects of life so that our community can lead a religious life that is suited to our context.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I applaud MUIS' efforts to publish a compilation of fatwa that not only serves as a source of reference, but also shows that we, as a minority Muslim community, are able to contribute to the development of global Islamic jurisprudence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The socio-religious needs of Malay/Muslims in Singapore are constantly met by our professional and competent group of asatizahs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Therefore, the quality of madrasah education will be enhanced further.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: At the National Day Rally in 2015, the Prime Minister expressed the Government's support for the teaching and learning of secular subjects in all six of our full-time madrasahs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As for religious subjects, MUIS will match the Government's support by introducing awards for students and training grants for teachers in religious subjects.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In addition, the Madrasah Al-Arabiah building will have a new look.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The balance will be co-funded by the madrasah and the community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I am grateful that MBMF, something that is uniquely Singapore, has been effectively supporting our socio-religious needs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: This shows that our community is getting more affluent and our gotong royong spirit is even stronger.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I agree that we want to achieve even more in all aspects of life in Singapore.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: But this will take time, and my colleagues and I are confident that all our efforts thus far will bring about the excellence that we want to achieve for our community.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: If a wave comes and spreads enmity, we unite to strengthen our friendship.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: When Singaporeans form friendships and kinships that are multicultural in nature, we embody the true meaning of diversity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: These norms and values reflect the stature and purity of thought.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: The experience of other countries is a lesson for us on the negative consequences when we fail to take into account the public good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: There will be uncertainty, suspicions will become rampant and the space for understanding will become narrower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: For me, wisdom is more meaningful than a burning desire that ignores what is appropriate for public good.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: That is why our Pioneer leaders display wisdom when resolving complex issues.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As the Malay saying goes, "When faced with a delicate problem, handle it carefully and wisely to avoid making it worse." As a small nation, Singapore is vulnerable to all kinds of uncertainties that can affect its stability.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Nonetheless, having a positive and far-sighted attitude has helped us overcome challenges and differences in a mature and sincere manner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: What is clear is that the Malay/Muslim community can take pride in our collective accomplishments and our contributions to Singapore over the past 52 years.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: So, let us continue to work together with the Government, to help one another and unite to overcome any obstacles with confidence, so as to create a brighter future for all of us.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: (In English): In closing, every one of us in our community has hopes and dreams for ourselves, our families and our children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: It was no different for our parents and grandparents, who had striven hard to forge a future in a new nation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Their future then is what we enjoy today.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: CCs are managed by local community leaders and volunteers.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They determine the mix of services and programmes in consultation with the residents.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Examples include social services, after school care, tuition and other forms of support.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: I can understand Assoc Prof Daniel Goh's concerns with the local tuition culture.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: There are many forms of tuition and student guidance services.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: They range from those providing help to (a) students who need more guidance to keep pace with their school work; (b) others who are pursuing excellence in some subjects.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The range of providers include volunteers helping less privileged students, as well as paid, organised classes.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: On the other hand, many other things will need to be done to change the broader tuition culture that Assoc Prof Daniel Goh speaks of.

speaker: The Minister, Prime Minister's Office (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our communities will have to determine the balance and the type of services that they wish to provide and access at all CCs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari
text: My clarification is for Mr Faisal Manap whether he is aware that there is actually a Malay Brigadier-General who is still actively serving in the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) as an NSman and he is Brigadier-General Ishak Ismail.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I just want to know what is the update on the assistance rendered to Madrasah Wat Tanjong at the current moment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Can I know which fund is MUIS tapping on?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Thirdly, can I also know whether there are any terms and conditions attached to this assistance?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Can I get a clarification from the Minister whether religious teachers from schools of thoughts other than from the mazhab will be officially recognised under ARS?

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: To the Member's first question, I cannot reveal the full details.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: We recognise that we want to assist Madrasah Wak Tanjong because it is part of our entire madrasah ecosystem.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Once the details are out on how we can work together to ensure that the lease for the space for Madrasah Wak Tanjong has been approved, we will announce the details.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I just have two clarifications following the Minister's announcement about Madrasah Al-Arabiah, which I think is good news.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: My first question is about the estimated completion time of Madrasah Al-Arabiah in Toa Payoh.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The second question is whether, with the new location, there will be an increase in student capacity in the new school.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: I must apologise I do not have the details of the timing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: But I suspect it will take about three years because we have to demolish the building.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: As I mentioned in my reply, we will consult with the mosque community on the design in the third quarter and, certainly, we will draw upon the Member's experience in Toa Payoh to help us also to see what is the best design possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: In terms of capacity, as you know, we have an intake of 400 every year.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: So, we have to design for the steady state.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: But at the secondary level, we do allow students coming from other systems to come in, too.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: But I have instructed MUIS to make sure that we plan it in such a way that if we want to expand to one or two more classes, we should have the capacity to do so.

speaker: Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim
text: Since we are building the building from fresh, from start, it is a green field, we might as well plan ahead for some additional capacity, just in case.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But work is needed to bring out this generosity.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And as our young society matures, we must establish the social norms that encourage our people to take care of one another, to build a shared future together, to create ties that bind us together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: To reword a famous phrase by Winston Churchill, "First we build a society, thereafter the society builds us".

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And no one group by themselves, including the Government, has a monopoly on the ideas to build an ideal Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: That is why I am heartened to see MCCY's emphasis on encouraging our citizens to step forward to co-create Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, can MCCY provide an update on how the Government is progressing to: one, encourage more Singapore Citizens to actively participate in volunteering and charity work?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Two, to partner with citizens, social service organisations (SSOs) and corporations?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Three, to move forward initiatives, such as Our Singapore Fund, SGCares, Champions of Good, and Company of Good Fellowship?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Volunteering connects our seniors to others in our community, provides fun and a sense of fulfilment, and benefits their mind and body.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many studies have found that volunteers report higher levels of happiness.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Researchers at the London School of Economics even discovered that the more people volunteered, the happier they were.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I understand many organisations encourage and express appreciation for their volunteers through various incentives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For example, museums invite their volunteers for previews and provide them with priority for shows.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We should acknowledge and recognise our senior volunteers' efforts more publicly and this will help draw even more seniors to our cause.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Singapore Fund (OSF) supports initiatives to bring our community together and promote our Singapore Spirit and shared values.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Government is providing funds to help firms internationalise and build capabilities to operate overseas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should do the same for our Institutions of a Public Character (IPCs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should support our local IPCs which internationalise, fly the Singapore flag proudly overseas and lend a helping hand to our neighbours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us be seen to not just venture into other countries to compete, to take, but to also give and to help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should let the public rather than the Government decide on how donations are spent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Within sight of one another are the Chulia Mosque, Sri Mariamman Temple, the Buddha Tooth Relic Temple and Fairfield Methodist Church, each unique in its faith tradition but integral parts of Singapore's short 50 years of being.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But we know from our own history that what we have today was born out of painful memories and a collective wish never to return to the tensions of the past.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We also only need to look around us and realise that things can change very dramatically.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Terrorism in Nice, Istanbul, Berlin, Paris, Jakarta, Baghdad.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Racial and religious tensions in Syria, Pakistan, Myanmar, even in the US.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Public places, including places of worship, can become targets.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When I am at my own parish church on Sundays, we have large numbers of visitors mixing easily and freely with regular parishioners, a reflection of the welcome and openness, but also revealing the troubling potential of becoming a "soft target".

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The same is true for many other places of worship, be they mosques, temples or churches.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Religious and community leaders have a special responsibility to speak up in times of crisis to convey messages of calm and solidarity to their respective congregations and, again, to the wider society.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: With 32 churches and almost 360,000 members, the Archdiocese of Singapore has been putting in place plans to ensure safety and preparedness for their congregations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The Archdiocese's emergency response operations team has also been actively sharing their experiences with other religious groups.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: MUIS, the Hindu Endowment Board, as well as the Singapore Buddhist Federation, also have their own teams in ensuring that their places of worship are kept secure and their congregations kept alert.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, the leadership of our various religious institutions need to make it a point to also reach out to leaders from other faith traditions.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because beyond plans and contingencies, it is the human-to-human relations that are the most important.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Trust cannot be built unless you know one another.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore, after all, is only 50 years young.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We envision a long road ahead, and our policies reflect that approach.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Getting to SG100 will not be without its challenges.

speaker: Mr Alex Yam (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But if we do it together and stand united in the face of adversity, we will survive and thrive.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Our perspectives and habits are formed through our experiences and interactions with the people around us.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Therefore, it is important to expose our young to the diversity of cultures and differences of opinions through organic platforms to help them develop more holistically.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: With such platforms, young people from different backgrounds can interact, learn about one another and have open and frank conversations about their differences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Clearly, the school is a natural platform for this purpose.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, there may be certain limitations in schools because of school hours or because the students from one school may be from a similar background.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In any case, I believe our bonds can be strengthened through sharing many more experiences together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: NS is a good example of a shared experience that has created strong bonds.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I have often envied my male family members and friends for having gone through NS.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There are, indeed, many avenues to create shared experiences through sports, outdoor activities and the arts and culture.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I note that many programmes and activities have already been put in place.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: It is not easy for our youths to grapple with, especially as this is a sudden change from the very positive employment market for fresh graduates until recently.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: When I graduated from university in 2000, my peers and I graduated into a recession.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: It was quite disorientating for us to go into university in a boom-time, only to graduate into a bleak employment situation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: We all know that the economy ebbs and flows and the future is likely more uncertain than the past.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: So, the answer is not to insulate our people completely from the uncertainty, because we cannot.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: The answer is to train our youths better to help them to be more resilient in all situations, including the employment situation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: One of the contentious issues debated was on the proposal to have a reserved minority Presidential Election.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The Constitutional Commission has mooted this proposal as they viewed that there is a need to address the issue of perceptions of minorities not able to access the highest office in the land.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The House was divided on this issue and so was the nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Those who supported this proposal argued that it is necessary to do so to symbolise Singapore's Constitution of multiculturalism.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: As for those who opposed it, the argument is that such implementation will undermine the principle of meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I am also of the view that the approach taken by the Government in mitigating the issue of perception of inequality by implementing a reserved Presidential Election for Malays shows that if the Government has the will to do and chooses to do it, it can be done.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I have said this a few times and I am going to repeat it again.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: One of the concerns of the Malay/Muslim community that is still lingering in our mind is the feeling of being discriminated, not being given equal and fair opportunity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: An example − there are still concerns from the community that a Malay individual is not able to assume the rank of a General in the army, a Permanent Secretary in the Ministries.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Minister Yaacob acknowledged these concerns during his interaction with tertiary students at a recent REACH-organised event.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: As I have mentioned earlier, when there is a will, there is a way.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I do sincerely hope that the Government will address the Malay/Muslim community's concerns in entirety.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, New Zealand offers a one-off temporary tax exemption for certain types of foreign income for returning New Zealanders who did not reside in the country for 10 years prior.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second point is on the management of the arts sector.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I think a free and vibrant arts scene is probably not the number one consideration for most people's migration decision but neither is it completely irrelevant.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Here, I would like to return to a theme I spoke about twice last year, which is, the conditions for Government support for the arts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In so doing, it reduces one liveability factor and makes Singapore that much less attractive as a home for all its people, regardless of political viewpoint.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This year, students took an active step by curating the exhibition on local festivals and local foods with Sun Yat Sen Memorial Hall and serving as student ambassadors to the million visitors who visited River Hongbao.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: From their happy and excited faces, I could tell that the students enjoyed and were proud of their efforts to co-curate our arts and heritage.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The experience of curating facts, interesting practices and unique displays of our arts and heritage can thus be a fun and learning experience for our students.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Through embarking on this across schools or even at a national level, they get to know the subject matter better and also appreciate the common experience and opportunities to get to know friends across the cohort.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This could be in the form of co-curricular activities (CCA) and can be guided by a teacher.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such collaborative efforts across schools can also promote bonding within cohorts and be a shared experience forming a collective memory for cohorts of students.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: The exposure to arts as well as heritage is an important component in ensuring the holistic education and development of our young.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In the local context, it is important in helping our children and youths understand and appreciate the different cultures in Singapore and build their national identity.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: We should, therefore, continue to build on these efforts and ensure that children and youths, regardless of social background, are given the same opportunities and exposure.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I feel it is easy enough to create generic programmes and platforms.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: It may be more difficult though to ensure meaningful appreciation of the arts and heritage, sustained participation as well as continued engagement.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: A meaningful programme should not just be about attending once-off art classes, museum tours or heritage trails.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There must be assessment of the impact of the programmes in reaching out to different groups in the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In particular, it is important to ensure that those from lower-income families also continue to have access to these programmes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: What more can be done to encourage these families to participate in the various arts and heritage programmes?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Arts and heritage activities add colour and vibrancy to our lives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: They are the perfect platforms for us to engage one another and help nurture our common identity and national unity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Hence, it is important that our arts and heritage programmes and spaces are available to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: In particular, we must reach out to vulnerable Singaporeans so that they, too, can participate fully in our cultural and community events.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Besides removing or lowering the barrier of entry fees, we should also invite them through sponsored trips to the sites of the activities.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Often, they are not even aware of them due to more pressing issues in their lives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: (In Mandarin):    I would like to suggest that we attract more seniors to our museums by offering tours in the vernacular languages and making the experience more interactive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: For example, at the end of the tours, there could be quizzes with prizes to add a bit of spice and fun.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Such formats will engage the visitors at a deeper level as the competition will spur them to pay attention and ask questions.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: If the tours could also involve youth volunteers, there would be good opportunities to promote intergenerational bonding.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One way is through sports, which brings Singaporeans from all walks of life together.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: On the playing field, regardless of our differences, we learn shared values like resilience, mutual respect, fair play and teamwork.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many of us played sports in school but, often, we are unable to find a suitable place to continue playing the sport together and we lose the camaraderie.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there any plans by the Ministry in the coming years to promote the creation of and participation in more sporting activities at the community level?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Beyond programmes, we also need spaces for communities to play sports together and foster social bonding.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Are there any upcoming plans under the Sports Facilities Master Plan to provide new spaces for more community use?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Can the Ministry consider conducting talks to graduating secondary and junior college students to encourage them to continue their sporting activities together after graduation?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We can start with the school's graduating sports teams.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A system to match these teams to community sports facilities within their own neighbourhood would allow them to continue playing together even after they graduate.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: While the memories are still fresh, I hope the Ministry will strike while the iron is hot and expand on the Disability Sports Master Plan (DSMP) and keep growing inclusive spaces for people with disabilities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Is the Ministry actively working closely with persons with disabilities to ensure their regular participation and enjoyment of sports, arts and culture?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The Government is doing a lot to support the likes of Yip Pin Xiu, but I hope non-competitive regular Singaporeans on the streets are also getting the help and push needed to participate in sports and also other cultural activities, to give persons with disabilities the opportunity to lead an active and enriching life.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We should see more facilities enabling barrier-free accessibility at places, such as sports stadiums, art galleries, cultural institutions, museums and so on.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Government legislate as well as to ensure all sports, heritage, arts and culture developments have inclusive spaces in mind?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: In this regard, schools have many sports facilities that are not used after school hours, such as indoor halls, basketball courts as well as the football fields.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: The public should be given greater access to use these facilities to support their sporting endeavours.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Opening more sports facilities in schools and Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) for use by the community is also beneficial, as it would reduce the need for new infrastructure to be built.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: How many schools have facilities under the Dual-Use Scheme?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Has there been progress since, and can we step up the opening of schools' sport facilities to meet the community's needs?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Is it possible to avail the sports facilities in all schools to the public after school hours on all weekday evenings?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye
text: Can the Ministry also consider upgrading the ActiveSG online portal and mobile app to help match last-minute cancellations of facilities bookings with people who have spontaneously decided to play the sport and are looking for an available venue?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Faisal Manap, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: For a period of 34 years, the former National Stadium had lived up to its name and status as a national icon.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: It has hosted a total of 18 National Day Parades (NDPs), two Southeast Asian Peninsular (SEAP) Games and one Southeast Asian (SEA) Games, and many memorable sporting tournaments, such as the Malaysia Cup.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: Our National Stadium was also the birthplace of our popular Kallang Wave.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I think everyone can attest to the fact that our former National Stadium had brought Singaporeans together, feeling the oneness, shedding tears of joy and despair, especially during the soccer matches that involved our national football team.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: It has been open for almost three years.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: I do hope that the Ministry will be able to facilitate in mitigating the present challenges faced by event organisers and our NSAs, especially FAS, so that 30 years down the road, Singaporeans will have the same recollections of fond and nostalgic memories similar to that of our first National Stadium.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: The last goal was set in 1988 by our former Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong, a popular one, indeed, Goal 2010, to qualify for the World Cup 2010.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: In reply, the Ministry said that there is a taskforce that is looking at setting out the goals and strategic directions for Singapore football in the coming years.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: In the Ministry's reply to my colleague Ms Sylvia Lim's query during the debate on the President's Address on 29 January 2016, it was mentioned that FAS would be having their annual general meeting (AGM) in June 2016.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The S-League is dying a slow and painful death.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It was not long ago that 60,000 Singaporeans were cheering on the national football team.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: As a fan and a journalist who covered the sport in the 1990s, I would like to suggest the reasons for this sad state of affairs are a lack of leadership and passion.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The 1970s and the 1990s were the golden era of local football, when the National Stadium was packed to the rafters and families were glued to their television (TVs) for "live" telecasts.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We idolised the players, legends like Quah Kim Song, the late Dollah Kassim, Mohammed Noor, Eric Paine, Fandi Ahmad and V Sundramoorthy.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: To me, however, both these periods owe their success primarily to two leaders.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In the 1970s and 1980s, it was the late Mr N Ganesan and, in the 1990s, it was former Cabinet Minister Mr Mah Bow Tan.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I had the privilege of knowing both these gentlemen.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I first met Mr N Ganesan in the early 1970s when I was about six or seven.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Ganesan was a family friend and he would be a frequent visitor to our home.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I used to look forward to his visits as he was fiercely passionate about football and told me endless stories about my local football idols.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Ganesan was a full-time lawyer but was at the Jalan Besar Stadium every day to watch the Lions train.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He was omnipresent, always available to speak to anyone, from players to coaches and staff at FAS.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And he created an air of camaraderie and family at FAS.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: And because his passion was so infectious, it caught on, creating a culture of volunteerism and selflessness that resulted in one of the most successful periods for local football.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The other more recent golden era of local football was the 1990s when Singapore won the Malaysia Cup in 1994.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We saw the birth of the S-League in 1996, and our famous Tiger Cup win in 1998.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I covered the 1993 and 1994 Malaysia Cup campaigns as well as the inaugural S-League season of 1996 as a journalist.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I remember Mr Mah as a quiet, stern leader, quite the opposite of Mr Ganesan in terms of personality.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But Mr Mah was a leader who got things done.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He brought a sense of purpose, discipline and work ethic to FAS.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Despite his hectic Ministerial duties, he would be present at most matches and training sessions.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: He ran a very tight ship, and this flowed through right down to the administration of the S-League and the clubs.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Things worked like clockwork − schedules, fixtures, press briefings.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: When Mr Mah briefed the media about the setting up of the S-League, there was a steely determination and resolve that said, "We will make this work".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It was an unenviable task during a difficult time.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Would we be able to replicate the success of the Malaysia Cup with our own fledgling league?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But after just a year of planning, Mr Mah oversaw the launch of the S-League in 1996.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Against all odds, Mr Mah had delivered on his promise, and our own professional football league was born.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, why have we come to where we are today?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: To me, there is a dearth of strong passionate leaders like the late Mr Ganesan and Mr Mah in local football.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: What we do not need is fair weather leadership.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Over the last few years, we have seen members of the FAS leadership team donning their jerseys and attending only big-ticket matches, but they are nowhere to be seen during training sessions or regular games.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen high-ranking FAS officials making trips across the globe and taking selfies with football superstars while the S-League is floundering.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen S-League clubs sign on washed-up, has-been, ill-disciplined foreign stars, garnering lots of press, but little else.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: These same clubs were having financial woes when they realised they had bitten off more than they can chew.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They would do well to remember the likes of Mohammed Khakpour and Hamid Reza Estili, the Iranian footballers who were foreign signings in the early days of the S-League.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: They were unknowns who became household names because of their dedication and quality.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Both players went on to represent Iran in the 1998 World Cup.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: At our height, we were ranked number 73 in the world, and this was only in 1993.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I am sure we can get there again.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Olympic medallist Joseph Schooling and Paralympians Theresa Goh and Yip Pin Xiu, among others, united us as a country and drew from us a collective roar of delight.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They made all of us feel proud to be Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that while we should continue to promote and support sporting excellence across the traditional sports, such as swimming, sailing, shooting and so on, however, I also believe that we should recognise achievements in other non-traditional sports where Singaporeans have excelled at a regional and international level.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Then, there are Singapore ice-skaters Chloe Ing and Yu Shuran who are making an impact in the regional figure-skating arena.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I know Minister Grace Fu featured Shuran on her Facebook page.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Sometimes, it is also about making that regional and international impact considered significant in a particular sport and not just look at the Olympics and world championships as a standard.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, l would suggest that we have other benchmarks, too.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While swimmers or runners can be assessed quantitatively by their timing, how do we benchmark athletes who have achieved in areas that cannot be measured quantitatively?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, could a young Singaporean tennis player who is regularly beating juniors in his or her age group in a country like Australia or the US be given more Government support?

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
